title: The triumphs of general relativity
one_line_summary: A short 'view from the summit' chapter closing Part II: it actually derives one payoff of the Einstein equation, the Newtonian weak-field limit that yields the metric -(1+2Phi)dt^2+(1-2Phi)dx^2 promised back in eqn 5.22, and then previews, mostly by quoting results and pictures, gravitational waves, Schwarzschild orbits with perihelion precession, black holes and Robertson-Walker cosmology.
role_in_book: Chapters 6-13 assembled the ingredients of general relativity (equivalence principle, metric, connection, curvature, energy-momentum tensor) and culminated in the field equation. Chapter 14 is the deliberate breather at the end of Part II. It discharges two outstanding obligations (Chapter 6's demand that the theory reduce to Newton, and the weak-field metric of eqn 5.22 that had been used without proof, e.g. for gravitational time dilation) and then acts as a trailer and road map for the rest of the spiral: Part III (cosmology, Robertson-Walker spaces), Part IV (Schwarzschild orbits, precession, light bending, black holes) and the Part VI chapters 45-46 that redo the weak-field limit and gravitational waves with gauge machinery. Almost everything here is stated at preview level, so it is also the first place a learner sees the whole landscape of GR's empirical successes at once.

assumed_background.topic: Einstein field equation G = 8 pi G T / c^4 and the Einstein tensor built from Ricci tensor and scalar
Trace reversal of a symmetric rank-2 tensor
assumed_background.where: GA ch13 §13.3 (Einstein tensor as trace-reversed Ricci)

assumed_background.topic: Perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor and mass/energy density
Minkowski metric, line elements, and raising/lowering indices with eta
The weak-field metric of eqn 5.22 (quoted there without derivation)
assumed_background.where: GA ch5; used in GA ch6 §6.5

assumed_background.topic: Tidal forces distort a freely falling sphere into an equal-volume ellipsoid; Riemann and Ricci tensors
Geometrized units G = c = 1 and the rules for restoring factors of c
Four-velocity components (gamma c, gamma u^i) and the Lorentz factor
Newtonian gravitational potential and Poisson's equation
Wave equation, plane-wave solutions e^{i(k.x - omega t)} and dispersion relations
Electromagnetic scalar and vector potentials, E and B from potentials, polarization of light
Effective-potential treatment of central-force orbits using energy and angular momentum conservation
Kepler orbits, perihelion, and basic Solar System astronomy

learning_objectives: Reader can state the weak-field criterion GM/(r c^2) << 1 and explain, by comparing v^2 with GM/r, why slow motion and weak gravity are the same approximation.
Reader can argue that for slowly moving, low-pressure matter the perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor collapses to T^{mu nu} ~ rho u^mu u^nu with T^{00} = rho c^2 dominating.
Reader can write the metric as eta plus a small perturbation h, define the trace-reversed perturbation h-bar and its trace property h-bar = -h, and quote the linearized field equation for h-bar.

Reader can reproduce the Example 14.2 chain: drop time derivatives, match to Poisson's equation to get h-bar_00 = -4 Phi, undo the trace reversal, and assemble ds^2 = -(1+2Phi)dt^2 + (1-2Phi)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2).

Reader can explain why vacuum Ricci-flatness forces tidal stretching and squeezing to balance, both for the tidal ellipsoid near a planet and for the one-stretch-one-squeeze pattern of a gravitational wave.
Reader can show that the source-free linearized equation is a wave equation and relate its plane-wave solutions to scalar and electromagnetic waves, including the idea of polarization.
Reader can sketch how a ring of free test masses deforms under the two gravitational-wave polarizations and how the pattern reverses every half period.
Reader can write the Schwarzschild line element and the relativistic effective potential, and identify the extra -G M L-tilde^2/(r^3 c^4) term as the relativistic correction.
Reader can read an effective-potential diagram with an energy line to classify motion as circular, bound and precessing, scattering, or plunging into the star.
Reader can list the three classical Solar System tests and quote Mercury's relativistic perihelion advance of about 43 arcseconds per century.
Reader can write the Robertson-Walker line element, say what a(t) and k = +1, 0, -1 represent, and describe the Big Bang as a singularity where classical GR stops applying.

teaching_approach.summary: A low-gradient survey framed as pausing at a mountain top after the climb to the field equation. Only one result is derived in full, the Newtonian limit, and it is done inside boxed examples with explicit 4x4 matrices and c set to 1, with the SI versions parked in a margin note. The remaining topics are presented as annotated results: gravitational waves are motivated by the 2015 LIGO detection, explained physically by reusing the Chapter 11 tidal-ellipsoid argument through Ricci-flatness, and formally by a ladder of wave equations borrowed from electromagnetism; orbits are handled with paired effective-potential and orbit-shape sketches; cosmology gets one metric and a paragraph. Every section ends with a boxed pointer to where the rigorous treatment lives.
narrative_arc: Summit framing: restate the field equation (14.1) in SI units and announce a chapter of payoffs rather than new machinery.
Pose the consistency check demanded in Chapter 6: does the field equation reduce to Newtonian gravity?
Make 'non-relativistic' precise: gamma ~ 1, u^0 >> u^i, and by dimensional analysis small GM/(r c^2).
Simplify the source (Example 14.1): pressure ~ rho v^2 is negligible against rho c^2, so only T^{00} matters.
Model the metric as Minkowski plus a small perturbation, introduce the trace-reversed h-bar, and quote the linearized equation (14.4).

Example 14.2: neglect time derivatives, compare with Poisson's equation, fix h-bar_00 = -4 Phi, invert the trace reversal with explicit matrices, and land on the metric (14.10), closing the IOU from eqn 5.22.
Switch to gravitational waves, motivated by LIGO's 2015 black-hole-merger detection.
Example 14.3: vacuum means R_{mu nu} = 0, which explains volume-preserving tides and implies a matched stretch-squeeze pair for waves.
Picture the two polarizations acting on a ring of test masses (Fig. 14.1), with the distortion reversing every half period.

Formal origin: with no source, eqn 14.4 becomes a wave equation (14.12); Example 14.4 builds up through scalar and 1-form (electromagnetic) waves to the plane-wave solution for h-bar (14.16) and notes the component count.
Quote the Schwarzschild line element (14.17), list the three classical tests in the margin, and introduce the effective-potential energy equation (14.18-14.19) with its relativistic 1/r^3 term.
Show the orbit zoo (Fig. 14.2) and the precessing rosette (Fig. 14.3); quote Mercury's 43 arcsec per century; mention light bending, lensing and black holes.
Cosmology: quote the Robertson-Walker metric (14.20), interpret k and a(t), mention the Big Bang as a singularity.
Summarize and signpost Part III (cosmology), Part IV (orbits and black holes), and Chapters 45-46.
signature_moves: Mountain-climb metaphor used to mark the end of tool-building and lower the learner's effort level before the applications parts.
Explicit debt repayment: the weak-field metric quoted in Chapter 5 is finally derived and the text says so.
Undoing the trace reversal by writing out full matrices, so the surprising equal -2 Phi in every diagonal slot is seen rather than asserted.
Working with c = 1 in the body and collecting all c-restored versions in a single margin note tagged (14.5).

Reusing the Chapter 11 tidal-ellipsoid bookkeeping to explain gravitational waves: planet tides stretch one axis and squeeze two, a wave stretches one and squeezes one, and Ricci-flatness balances both.
A ladder of wave equations (scalar, then 1-form/electromagnetic, then symmetric two-index h-bar) where polarization grows richer with the number of indices.
Each effective-potential sketch is placed beside the orbit shape it produces, with the energy line and turning points marked.
Boxed forward pointers at the end of each section naming the chapter or part where the full treatment lives.

sections.title: Chapter opening: the view from the summit
sections.summary: After an epigraph from Gibbon about ambition, the authors restate the field equation in SI units as the peak of a long climb and announce that this chapter only surveys what the theory achieves, with details deferred to later parts.
key_moves: Field equation (14.1) displayed with 8 pi G/c^4
Chapter framed as a review of successes rather than new machinery

sections.title: Weak fields and the Newtonian limit
sections.summary: Defines the regime where Newton should re-emerge (slow motion, equivalently weak potentials GM/(r c^2) small), reduces a perfect fluid to its mass-density component, writes the metric as flat plus a small perturbation, and uses the trace-reversed perturbation in the linearized field equation. Matching the static 00 component to Poisson's equation gives h-bar_00 = -4 Phi; reversing the trace gives every diagonal perturbation equal to -2 Phi, hence the weak-field line element of eqn 5.22. A margin note restores all factors of c.
key_moves: Slow motion means |u|^2/c^2 << 1, so gamma ~ 1 and u^0 >> u^i
Since particle speeds are set by v^2 ~ GM/r, slow motion is equivalent to GM/(r c^2) << 1
p ~ rho v^2 << rho c^2, so T^{mu nu} ~ rho u^mu u^nu and T^{00} dominates
g = eta + h with |h| << 1; indices moved with eta; h is not a true tensor
Trace reverse h-bar = h - (1/2) eta h makes the linearized equation box h-bar = -16 pi G T/c^4
Static source: drop time derivatives, get del^2 h-bar_00 = -16 pi G rho; other components source-free and vanish at infinity
Compare with del^2 Phi = 4 pi G rho: h-bar_00 = -4 Phi, h-bar = +4 Phi
Invert the trace reversal: h = diag(-2Phi,-2Phi,-2Phi,-2Phi), giving ds^2 = -(1+2Phi)dt^2 + (1-2Phi)dx^2

sections.title: Gravitational waves
sections.summary: Introduces gravitational waves as ripples of the metric that move free masses, notes that their tiny effects went undetected until LIGO saw a 150 ms burst from merging black holes in 2015, and gives two explanations. Physically, the vacuum field equation reduces to R_{mu nu} = 0, which forces stretching and squeezing to cancel: near a planet this is the equal-volume tidal ellipsoid (one stretch, two squeezes of half size) and for a wave it is one stretch balanced by one equal squeeze. Pictorially, a ring of test masses oscillates between perpendicular ellipses in two polarizations. Formally, the source-free linearized equation is a wave equation, and a ladder from scalar to electromagnetic waves motivates plane-wave solutions for h-bar whose multiple components produce polarization.
concepts: Ricci tensor as the volume-changing part of curvature
independent components of a symmetric tensor
key_moves: Field equation is local: where T vanishes, R_{mu nu} - (1/2) g R vanishes, hence R_{mu nu} = 0 in vacuum
Ricci is the trace-like contraction of Riemann that controls volume change, so vacuum tides preserve volume
Planet tides: stretch along one axis, squeeze half as strongly along two axes; the budget balances
Wave: stretch along one transverse axis, equal squeeze along the other
Ring of test masses flips its elongation every half period; two polarizations rotated by 45 degrees
Vacuum linearized equation: box h-bar_{mu nu} = 0, a wave equation
Scalar wave, then 1-form wave with polarization vector C_mu, then E and B from potentials
Plane-wave h-bar = Re[A e^{ik.x}]; symmetry cuts 16 components to 10, and this multi-component structure underlies the polarizations

sections.title: Stars, trajectories, and orbits
sections.summary: Quotes the Schwarzschild line element for the vacuum outside a static spherical mass, lists the three classical tests, and treats radial motion as a particle rolling in a relativistic effective potential that adds an attractive 1/r^3 term to the Newtonian gravity plus centrifugal terms. Paired sketches show circular orbits, a scattering encounter, a plunge into the star, and a bound orbit whose ellipse precesses, with Mercury's 43 arcseconds per century as the historic success. Light bending, lensing and black holes are mentioned as further consequences.
key_moves: Outside the mass T = 0, so the Schwarzschild metric solves G = 0
Energy-like first integral E = (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 + V_eff(r)
V_eff = Newtonian gravity term + centrifugal term + relativistic -GML^2/r^3 term
Energy line versus V_eff shape classifies orbits: at the minimum (circular), between walls (precessing bound), below the peak from outside (scatter), above the peak (capture)
Precession is the slow rotation of the near-ellipse; Mercury gives ~43.0 arcsec per century in agreement with observation
A similar effective potential for light predicts bending and lensing; very compact masses give black holes

sections.title: Cosmology
sections.summary: Extends the reach of the field equation to the whole Universe through the Robertson-Walker line element, whose spatial part is scaled by a time-dependent a(t) and whose constant k = +1, 0, -1 sets spatial curvature. Different matter contents give different histories, many beginning in a Big Bang singularity where classical theory fails. The chapter summary then lists the four headline results and points to Part III.
key_moves: Spatial geometry that changes with cosmic time t gives cosmic evolution
Dynamics reduce to equations of motion for the single function a(t)
Many model universes start from a = 0, a singularity where GR breaks down

sections.title: Chapter summary
sections.summary: Four bullets restate the chapter's claims: Newton is recovered for weak fields, gravitational waves are excitations of the metric field, GR turns closed Newtonian ellipses into precessing near-ellipses, and cosmology describes the Universe's origin and fate.
key_moves: Recap only; forward pointer to Part III

concepts.name: Einstein field equation
concepts.definition: The equation of general relativity setting the Einstein tensor (a combination of the Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar built from the metric) proportional to the energy-momentum tensor, with coupling 8 pi G / c^4 in SI units.
concepts.how_introduced: Restated at the start as the summit reached at the end of Chapter 13, then written again in component form R_{mu nu} - (1/2) g_{mu nu} R = 8 pi G T_{mu nu}/c^4 in Example 14.3 to stress that it is a local equation at each spacetime point.

concepts.name: weak-field limit
concepts.definition: The regime in which the metric differs only slightly from Minkowski and the gravitational potential is small compared with c^2, i.e. GM/(r c^2) << 1; bodies moving under such gravity acquire speeds v with v^2/c^2 << 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the slow-motion condition |u|^2/c^2 << 1 (so gamma ~ 1 and u^0 >> u^i) and then translated by dimensional analysis: gravitationally induced speeds satisfy v^2 ~ GM/r, so slowness and weakness are the same small parameter.
concepts.notes: The printed criterion (GM/rc)^2 << 1 is dimensionally inconsistent; the intended dimensionless parameter is GM/(r c^2).

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of general relativity
concepts.definition: The requirement, and the demonstration, that for weak static fields and slowly moving low-pressure matter the Einstein equation reduces to Poisson's equation with g_00 = -(1 + 2 Phi/c^2), so geodesic motion reproduces Newtonian gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as fulfilling a design requirement laid down in Chapter 6; carried out via the linearized equation and Poisson matching in Example 14.2.

concepts.name: non-relativistic energy-momentum tensor
aliases: pressureless limit of a perfect fluid
concepts.definition: For matter whose internal speeds are small, pressure p ~ rho v^2 is negligible compared with rho c^2, so the perfect-fluid tensor reduces to T^{mu nu} ~ rho u^mu u^nu, and because u^0 >> u^i the component T^{00} = rho c^2 dwarfs the others.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 14.1 restores factors of c in the perfect-fluid tensor and uses a margin note that estimates pressure as the kinetic energy density of particles striking container walls.
formulas: T^{\mu\nu} \approx \rho u^\mu u^\nu,\ T^{00}=\rho c^2 \gg T^{ii}

concepts.name: slow-motion approximation of the four-velocity
concepts.definition: When |u|/c is small, gamma is essentially 1 and the four-velocity (gamma c, gamma u^i) is dominated by its time component, so terms containing spatial velocity components can be dropped relative to those containing u^0.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the opening of §14.1 as the working meaning of non-relativistic, then used to justify keeping only T^{00}.

concepts.name: metric perturbation
concepts.definition: The small symmetric array h_{mu nu} = g_{mu nu} - eta_{mu nu} with |h_{mu nu}| << 1 describing a weak gravitational field; its indices are raised and lowered with the flat metric eta, and it behaves as a tensor only under background Lorentz transformations, shifting under infinitesimal coordinate changes.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the natural model of a weak field once the Newtonian regime is defined, with a caution that h is not really a tensor, to be explained later.
concepts.notes: The book only asserts the non-tensor status; gauge (coordinate) freedom that explains it is deferred to GA ch45.

concepts.name: trace-reversed metric perturbation
concepts.definition: The combination h-bar_{mu nu} = h_{mu nu} - (1/2) eta_{mu nu} h, where h = eta^{mu nu} h_{mu nu}; in four dimensions its trace is minus that of h, so applying the same operation twice returns h, giving h_{mu nu} = h-bar_{mu nu} - (1/2) eta_{mu nu} h-bar.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the variable in which the linearized field equation looks simplest, linked by a margin note to the trace reversal met in Chapter 13, and then inverted explicitly with 4x4 matrices in Example 14.2.

concepts.name: linearized Einstein equation
concepts.definition: To first order in h, and in a suitable gauge, the Einstein equation becomes a flat-space wave equation for the trace-reversed perturbation sourced by the energy-momentum tensor: box h-bar_{mu nu} = -16 pi G T_{mu nu}/c^4.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without derivation as what comes out after inserting g = eta + h into the field equation; used for both the Newtonian limit and gravitational waves.
concepts.notes: Valid only after imposing the Lorenz (harmonic) gauge condition partial^mu h-bar_{mu nu} = 0, which this chapter does not mention.

concepts.name: d'Alembertian operator
concepts.definition: The Lorentz-invariant second-order operator eta^{mu nu} partial_mu partial_nu = -(1/c^2) partial_t^2 + del^2; setting it to zero on a field gives the wave equation, and for static fields it reduces to the Laplacian.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in eqn 14.4 and unpacked in Example 14.2 to justify dropping the time derivative for slow sources, then written out in components for a scalar field in Example 14.4.

concepts.name: Poisson equation for gravity
concepts.definition: Newton's field equation relating the gravitational potential to mass density, del^2 Phi = 4 pi G rho.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the target: comparing it with the static 00 component of the linearized equation fixes h-bar_00 = -4 Phi (or -4 Phi/c^2 in SI).

concepts.name: weak-field metric
concepts.definition: The approximate metric of a weak static gravitational field with Newtonian potential Phi: ds^2 = -(1 + 2Phi/c^2)c^2 dt^2 + (1 - 2Phi/c^2)(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2); both the time and the space parts are modified by the same potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived as the payoff of Example 14.2 by assembling eta plus the perturbation diag(-2Phi, -2Phi, -2Phi, -2Phi), and explicitly identified as the proof of the metric quoted in Chapter 5.
concepts.notes: The spatial (1 - 2Phi) factor is what doubles the Newtonian estimate of light deflection; the chapter does not draw this out.

concepts.name: restoring factors of c
aliases: dimensional bookkeeping between geometrized and SI units
concepts.definition: Translating equations written with c = 1 back to SI by inserting powers of c so that each term has consistent dimensions (e.g. Phi becomes Phi/c^2 in the metric, T^{00} becomes rho c^2).
concepts.how_introduced: The section explicitly keeps c visible because the limit is about speeds compared with c; Example 14.2 sets c = 1 and a margin note (tagged 14.5) supplies the SI versions, pointing to dimensional analysis or the Chapter 0 table.

concepts.name: gravitational waves
concepts.definition: Propagating, source-free oscillations of the metric perturbation that travel at c and produce periodic transverse tidal distortions of freely falling matter, alternately stretching and squeezing distances in perpendicular directions.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by analogy with electromagnetic waves and by the 2015 LIGO detection; explained physically via Ricci-flat tidal balance (Example 14.3), pictured with rings of test masses (Fig. 14.1), and formally as solutions of the vacuum linearized equation.

concepts.name: vacuum Ricci-flatness
concepts.definition: Where there is no energy-momentum, the Einstein equation forces the Ricci tensor to vanish, although the full Riemann tensor (and hence tidal effects) can be non-zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 14.3 writes the field equation with explicit x-dependence to stress that it holds event by event; where T vanishes the right-hand side vanishes, and the book jumps straight to R_{mu nu} = 0. The skipped step (tracing to get R = 0 first) is worth supplying for learners.

concepts.name: Ricci tensor as the volume-changing part of curvature
concepts.definition: The contraction R_{mu nu} = R^alpha_{mu alpha nu} of the Riemann tensor; it measures the part of curvature that makes a small ball of initially comoving free particles change volume, while the remaining (Weyl) part changes only its shape.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin note as a kind of average of Riemann that keeps the volume-shrinking information, then used to explain why vacuum tides conserve volume.
concepts.notes: The Weyl-tensor language is ours; the book says only that Ricci retains the volume-shrinking part.

concepts.name: volume-preserving tidal deformation
concepts.definition: In vacuum, a small freely falling sphere of test particles is distorted by tides into an ellipsoid of the same volume: stretching along some directions is exactly compensated by compression along others. Near a planet the stretch along the radial line is twice the squeeze along each of the two perpendicular axes.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 11 at the start of Example 14.3 and re-explained using vacuum Ricci-flatness, with a margin note doing the one-stretch versus two half-size squeezes arithmetic.
formulas: \text{stretch } 2\epsilon \text{ along } r,\ \text{squeeze } \epsilon \text{ along each transverse axis}

concepts.name: gravitational-wave polarization
concepts.definition: The two independent patterns in which a gravitational wave distorts a ring of free masses in the plane transverse to propagation: one elongates it alternately along two perpendicular axes (plus), the other does the same along axes rotated by 45 degrees (cross).
concepts.how_introduced: Shown in Fig. 14.1(b) and (c) after the tidal-balance argument, and linked to the polarization of electromagnetic waves through the component structure of the wave amplitude.
concepts.notes: The names plus/cross, the 45 degree relation and the count of two physical polarizations are our additions; the book only says there are different polarizations.

concepts.name: wave equation
concepts.definition: A second-order equation stating that the d'Alembertian of a field vanishes; its solutions are disturbances travelling at speed c, built from plane waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Recognized in eqn 14.12 as what eqn 14.4 becomes with no matter, then illustrated for a scalar field in components (14.13) and for a 1-form (14.14).

concepts.name: plane-wave solution
concepts.definition: A solution of the wave equation of the form amplitude times exp[-i(omega t - k.x)] (real part taken), with omega = c|k|; for multi-component fields the amplitude carries indices that encode polarization.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 14.4 lists scalar, 1-form and then symmetric 2-index versions, taking real parts for physical fields.
formulas: \phi = C e^{-i(\omega t - \vec k\cdot\vec x)},\ \omega = c|\vec k|

concepts.name: electromagnetic four-potential
concepts.definition: The 1-form field A_mu whose time component is the electric scalar potential and whose spatial part is the vector potential; E = -grad A^0 - dA/dt and B = curl A.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in Example 14.4 as the familiar middle rung between scalar and gravitational waves, with a pointer to Chapter 42.
formulas: \vec E = -\vec\nabla A^0 - \frac{\partial\vec A}{\partial t},\ \vec B = \vec\nabla\times\vec A

concepts.name: independent components of a symmetric tensor
concepts.definition: A two-index object in four dimensions has 16 components; symmetry under index swap leaves 10 independent ones (and gauge freedom reduces the physically radiative ones for waves to 2).
concepts.how_introduced: A margin note counts 16 to 10 to explain why the h-bar field is more complicated than the electromagnetic potential.
concepts.notes: The reduction to 2 physical polarizations is not stated in this chapter.

concepts.name: LIGO detection of gravitational waves
concepts.definition: The 2015 observation by the two LIGO laser-interferometer detectors of a short gravitational-wave burst from the merger of two black holes, the first direct detection of such waves.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens §14.2 as the reason waves matter: their effects are so small that only an extremely powerful event could be seen.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The exact vacuum solution of the Einstein equation outside a static, spherically symmetric mass M, written in spherical coordinates with metric functions (1 - 2GM/(r c^2)) multiplying dt^2 and its inverse multiplying dr^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted, not derived, as one of the few known exact solutions and the basis of Solar System tests; the text notes it satisfies G = 0 outside the source.

concepts.name: relativistic effective potential
concepts.definition: A function of r whose sum with half the squared radial proper velocity is a conserved effective energy per unit mass, reducing Schwarzschild geodesic motion to one-dimensional motion; it contains the Newtonian gravity and centrifugal terms plus an extra attractive term proportional to M L^2 / r^3.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by analogy with Newton's central-force problem; the extra term is singled out as the relativistic correction and its consequences are shown in Figs 14.2-14.3.
concepts.notes: As printed, V_eff is dimensionless but (dr/dtau)^2/2 is a speed squared. The V_eff matches GA eqn 22.24 (overall 1/c^2), so the kinetic term needs 1/c^2 too; with G = c = 1 (GA eqns 22.22-22.23) everything is consistent.

concepts.name: specific angular momentum
concepts.definition: The conserved angular momentum of an orbiting body divided by its mass; its value sets the height and shape of the centrifugal barrier and thus which orbits are possible.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when V_eff is written, and emphasized as the conserved quantity on which the allowed trajectories depend.

concepts.name: orbit classification by effective potential
concepts.definition: Comparing a body's conserved effective energy with the effective potential: energy at the well minimum gives a circular orbit, energy inside the well gives bound motion between two turning radii, positive energy below the inner peak gives scattering, and energy above the peak gives capture.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown entirely through the paired potential and orbit sketches of Figs 14.2 and 14.3, with dots marking the relevant turning points.

concepts.name: perihelion precession
concepts.definition: The gradual rotation of the major axis of a bound, nearly elliptical orbit, so that successive closest approaches occur at advancing angles; in GR it arises because the radial and angular oscillation periods differ slightly.
concepts.how_introduced: Singled out as the most striking of the allowed orbits, drawn as a rosette in Fig. 14.3, and tied to Mercury as an early triumph of the theory.

concepts.name: classical tests of general relativity
concepts.definition: The three historic Solar System confirmations of GR: Mercury's anomalous perihelion advance, the deflection of starlight by the Sun, and gravitational redshift.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in a shaded margin box beside the Schwarzschild metric; only the first is discussed.

concepts.name: gravitational light bending
concepts.definition: The bending of light paths by a mass, following from null geodesics in curved spacetime; it produces gravitational lensing.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned after precession: an effective potential for light, analogous to the massive-particle one, predicts deflection and lensing.
concepts.notes: The text contrasts this with Newtonian theory; strictly, a Newtonian corpuscle argument gives half the GR deflection.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift
concepts.definition: The shift to lower frequency of light climbing out of a gravitational potential, equivalently the slower ticking of clocks deeper in the potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only in the margin list of classical tests.

concepts.name: black hole
concepts.definition: A region of spacetime around a sufficiently compact mass from which nothing, not even light, can escape.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned at the end of §14.3 as the extreme of Schwarzschild geometry for very dense sources, with a pointer to Part IV.

concepts.name: cosmology
concepts.definition: The use of general relativity to model the geometry of the Universe as a whole, and thereby its large-scale evolution, how it began and how it may end.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the widest-scale use of the field equation, beyond single-body trajectories.

concepts.name: Robertson-Walker metric
concepts.definition: The metric of a homogeneous, isotropic universe: ds^2 = -c^2 dt^2 + a(t)^2 [dr^2/(1 - k r^2) + r^2 dOmega^2], with cosmic time t, a scale factor a(t) and curvature constant k.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as the geometry of many model universes; its key feature is that the spatial part changes with t, giving cosmic evolution.

concepts.name: scale factor
concepts.definition: The function a(t) in the Robertson-Walker metric that multiplies all spatial distances between comoving points; its time dependence encodes the expansion or contraction of the Universe, and its equations of motion follow from the field equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Described informally as a sort of effective radius whose dynamics govern the model universe.
concepts.notes: Calling a(t) a radius only makes literal sense for k = +1; for k = 0 or -1 the space can be infinite.

concepts.name: spatial curvature parameter k
concepts.definition: The constant k = +1, 0 or -1 in the Robertson-Walker metric that selects spatially closed (spherical), flat, or open (hyperbolic) geometry of constant-time slices.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated alongside eqn 14.20 as the parameter distinguishing curvature types.
concepts.notes: The text says k describes the curvature of spacetime; more precisely it fixes the curvature of spatial slices.

concepts.name: Big Bang singularity
concepts.definition: The limit a(t) -> 0 reached in the past by many model universes, where curvature and density diverge and classical general relativity ceases to be a valid description.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as a notable feature of model universes and as an example of a spacetime singularity.

concepts.name: field excitation
concepts.definition: A travelling disturbance of a field (a wave solution of its field equation) carrying a finite, non-zero amount of energy; gravitational waves are presented as the excitations of the metric perturbation in the same sense as waves of a scalar or electromagnetic field.
concepts.how_introduced: Emphasized in bold inside Example 14.4 for the scalar field, then transferred to h-bar in the following paragraph and repeated in the chapter summary's description of gravitational waves.
concepts.notes: The word hints at the field-quantization view developed in Part VI; here it is used classically.

concepts.name: spacetime singularity
concepts.definition: A place in spacetime where a classical field theory such as general relativity stops giving a sensible description, typically because curvature or density grows without bound.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in passing, with the Big Bang offered as the example, at the end of §14.4.
concepts.notes: The book calls it a point in spacetime; for the Big Bang it is better thought of as a boundary (a whole spacelike slice at a = 0), not a location in space. See GA ch16 §16.4 and ch19 §19.3.

key_equations.name: Einstein field equation (SI, index-free)
key_equations.meaning: Curvature, via the Einstein tensor, equals the energy-momentum content times the coupling 8 pi G/c^4.
key_equations.symbols: G (bold) Einstein tensor; T (bold) energy-momentum tensor; G Newton's constant

key_equations.name: Slow-motion conditions
key_equations.latex: \frac{|\vec u|^2}{c^2}\ll 1,\quad \gamma\approx 1,\quad u^\mu=(\gamma c,\gamma u^i),\ u^0\gg u^i
key_equations.meaning: Working definition of non-relativistic motion and its consequence for four-velocity components.
key_equations.symbols: u^i three-velocity components; gamma Lorentz factor

key_equations.name: Weak-field criterion
key_equations.meaning: Gravity is weak when the Newtonian potential is small compared with c^2; equivalent to slow motion because v^2 ~ GM/r. Printed as (GM/rc)^2 << 1, which has dimensions of speed squared and should be read as (v/c)^2 ~ GM/(r c^2) << 1.

key_equations.latex:

key_equations.meaning: Pressure is negligible for slow matter, so the source is effectively dust dominated by its energy density.
key_equations.symbols: rho mass density; p pressure; v typical internal speed

key_equations.name: Weak-field decomposition
key_equations.meaning: Metric equals flat metric plus a small perturbation; perturbation indices moved with eta.
key_equations.symbols: eta Minkowski metric diag(-1,1,1,1); h perturbation

key_equations.name: Trace-reversed perturbation
key_equations.meaning: Defines the variable in which the linearized field equation is cleanest.

key_equations.name: Trace property (margin note 4)
key_equations.meaning: In four dimensions trace reversal flips the sign of the trace, so the operation is its own inverse.

key_equations.name: Linearized Einstein equation
key_equations.meaning: To first order (in Lorenz gauge, unstated here) the perturbation obeys a sourced flat-space wave equation.

key_equations.name: Static 00 component
key_equations.meaning: With c = 1, only T_00 = rho matters and time derivatives are negligible, leaving a Poisson-type equation.

key_equations.name: Matching to Newton
key_equations.meaning: Comparison with Poisson's equation fixes the only non-zero component; source-free components vanish given fall-off at infinity.

key_equations.name: Inverse trace reversal
key_equations.meaning: Recovers the metric perturbation from its trace-reversed version.

key_equations.name: Perturbation for a Newtonian source
key_equations.meaning: Every diagonal component of the perturbation equals -2 Phi: the spatial part is perturbed as much as the temporal part.

key_equations.name: c-restored weak-field relations (margin note 5)
key_equations.latex: T^{00}=\rho c^2,\quad \nabla^2\bar h_{00}=-\frac{16\pi G}{c^2}\rho,\quad \bar h_{00}=-4\Phi/c^2,\quad g_{00}=-(1+2\Phi/c^2)
key_equations.meaning: SI versions of the Example 14.2 results; eqn number sits in the margin, out of sequence with the main text.

key_equations.name: Full weak-field metric matrix
key_equations.meaning: Flat metric plus the Newtonian perturbation.

key_equations.name: Weak-field line element
key_equations.meaning: The metric of a weak static field (c = 1; Phi carries G), proving eqn 5.22; the dt^2 part gives Newtonian gravity and time dilation, the spatial part matters for light.

key_equations.name: Field equation in components
key_equations.meaning: Written with explicit x to stress locality: it holds separately at each event.
key_equations.symbols: R_{mu nu} Ricci tensor; R Ricci scalar

key_equations.name: Ricci contraction (margin note 7)
key_equations.meaning: Ricci tensor as a contraction (loosely an average) of Riemann that carries volume-changing information.

key_equations.name: Vacuum field equation
key_equations.meaning: Empty space is Ricci-flat, which forces tidal stretches and squeezes to balance.

key_equations.name: Vacuum linearized equation
key_equations.meaning: Without sources each component of h-bar obeys the wave equation: gravitational waves travelling at c.

key_equations.name: Scalar wave equation
key_equations.meaning: Component form of box phi = 0.

key_equations.name: Scalar plane wave and dispersion
key_equations.meaning: Plane waves solve the wave equation provided frequency and wavenumber are tied by omega = c|k|.
key_equations.symbols: C amplitude; k wavevector; omega angular frequency

key_equations.name: 1-form plane wave
key_equations.meaning: A vector-valued wave whose component ratios C_mu define polarization.

key_equations.name: Fields from potentials
key_equations.latex: \vec E=-\vec\nabla A^0-\frac{\partial\vec A}{\partial t},\qquad \vec B=\vec\nabla\times\vec A
key_equations.meaning: How familiar electric and magnetic fields follow from the 4-potential wave.

key_equations.name: Gravitational plane wave
key_equations.meaning: Plane-wave solution for the trace-reversed perturbation; the symmetric amplitude A_{mu nu} (10 components, 2 physical after gauge fixing) encodes polarization.
key_equations.symbols: A_{mu nu} polarization tensor; k.x = -omega t + k.x with signature (-+++)

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild line element
key_equations.meaning: Exact vacuum geometry outside a static spherical mass.

key_equations.name: Radial energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Geodesic motion reduces to a particle in one dimension with conserved effective energy.
key_equations.symbols: tau proper time; E effective energy per unit mass

key_equations.name: Relativistic effective potential
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian gravity term plus centrifugal barrier plus a relativistic attractive 1/r^3 term that creates an inner peak, allows plunging orbits and causes precession. As printed, V_eff is dimensionless while (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 in (14.18) is a speed squared. GA eqn 22.24 gives this same V_eff written with an overall 1/c^2, so the kinetic term in (14.18) also needs a 1/c^2 (or work in G = c = 1 as in eqns 22.22-22.23).
key_equations.symbols: L-tilde angular momentum per unit mass

key_equations.name: Mercury's relativistic perihelion advance
key_equations.meaning: Quoted value of the GR contribution to Mercury's precession, matching observation.

key_equations.name: Robertson-Walker line element
key_equations.meaning: Homogeneous isotropic cosmological geometry whose spatial size evolves through a(t).
key_equations.symbols: a(t) scale factor; k = +1, 0, -1 curvature constant

figures.label: Fig. 14.1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The reference configuration: test masses arranged on a circle in flat spacetime before any wave arrives.
figures.visual_description: Roughly sixteen equally spaced solid black dots sitting on a thin solid circle; no axes or labels other than the panel letter (a).
figures.what_it_teaches: Sets the undisturbed baseline against which the wave-induced distortions in panels (b) and (c) are judged.

redesign.idea: Gravitational-wave ring lab: a ring (or a 2D disc grid) of free masses in the transverse plane, driven by a wave whose plus and cross amplitudes and phase the learner controls, with ghost markers at the undisturbed positions and displacement arrows. This panel is the amplitude-zero state of that demo.
redesign.interaction: Start at zero amplitude to show the circle; a 'wave arrives' button ramps amplitude up so the learner sees the departure from this baseline.

figures.label: Fig. 14.1(b), first time
figures.caption_paraphrase: One polarization of a passing wave at one instant: the ring is squeezed horizontally and stretched vertically.
figures.visual_description: A dotted circle marks the original positions. Short arrows run from the circle to displaced black dots: dots at top and bottom are pushed outward, dots at left and right pulled inward, and dots at the diagonals slide roughly along the circle toward the vertical axis, giving an ellipse elongated vertically. Area appears unchanged.
figures.what_it_teaches: A gravitational wave produces one stretch and one equal squeeze at right angles in the plane transverse to propagation; this is the plus-type pattern.

redesign.idea: Gravitational-wave ring lab: a ring (or a 2D disc grid) of free masses in the transverse plane, driven by a wave whose plus and cross amplitudes and phase the learner controls, with ghost markers at the undisturbed positions and displacement arrows. Overlay a live bar showing the fractional stretch along x and y and their sum, which stays zero to first order.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for h_plus, h_cross, frequency and exaggeration factor; play/pause and scrub the phase; toggle displacement arrows and an area readout; click a mass to plot its displacement versus time.

figures.label: Fig. 14.1(b), half period later
figures.caption_paraphrase: The same polarization half a wave period later: the stretch and squeeze have swapped axes.
figures.visual_description: Dotted reference circle with arrows to displaced dots: now the leftmost and rightmost dots are pushed outward and the top and bottom dots pulled inward, producing an ellipse elongated horizontally. (The inventory attaches the full Fig. 14.1 caption to this image, but it is only the lower panel of (b).)
figures.what_it_teaches: The distortion oscillates: at a fixed place the elongation axis alternates every half period, equivalently every half wavelength along the propagation direction.

redesign.idea: Same ring lab with a split view: a strip along the propagation direction showing rings at several positions simultaneously, so the half-wavelength flip in space is seen alongside the half-period flip in time.
redesign.interaction: Scrub time or drag along the propagation axis; highlight which rings are in the vertical versus horizontal phase; readout of phase kz - omega t.

figures.label: Fig. 14.1(c), first time
figures.caption_paraphrase: The other polarization at one instant: the ring is stretched along one diagonal and squeezed along the other.
figures.visual_description: Dotted circle with displacement arrows to black dots. Dots in the upper-right and lower-left are displaced outward, those in the upper-left and lower-right inward, while dots at the top, bottom, left and right move nearly tangentially (e.g. the top dot slides right, the right dot slides up), forming an ellipse along the NE-SW diagonal.
figures.what_it_teaches: The second independent polarization is the first rotated by 45 degrees, not 90 degrees as for light; tangential arrows at the axes show the pattern is a shear rather than a radial pulse.

redesign.idea: Polarization rotator: a single dial sets the polarization angle psi of a linearly polarized wave; the learner discovers that rotating by 45 degrees turns plus into cross and 90 degrees merely flips the sign, contrasted with an electromagnetic dipole antenna panel where 90 degrees gives the orthogonal state.
redesign.interaction: Rotate the polarization dial; toggle EM comparison; add a phase offset between plus and cross to produce circular polarization where the elongation axis rotates.

figures.label: Fig. 14.1(c), half period later
figures.caption_paraphrase: The cross-type polarization half a period later: elongation has moved to the other diagonal.
figures.visual_description: Dotted circle with arrows to displaced dots; the ring is now elongated along the NW-SE diagonal, with upper-left and lower-right dots pushed out and upper-right and lower-left pulled in.
figures.what_it_teaches: Completes the oscillation for the second polarization, reinforcing the stretch-squeeze swap every half period.

redesign.idea: Fold into the ring lab as a phase snapshot; add a LIGO-arm overlay (two perpendicular arms) whose length difference is plotted, showing that an L-shaped detector responds fully to one polarization at a given orientation.
redesign.interaction: Rotate the detector arms relative to the polarization axes and watch the arm-length difference signal amplitude change.

figures.label: Fig. 14.2(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A circular orbit corresponds to sitting exactly at the bottom of the relativistic effective-potential well.
figures.visual_description: Left: axes labelled V_eff(r) (vertical) and |r| (horizontal) with a tick at 0. The curve plunges to large negative values very close to the vertical axis, rises steeply to a narrow positive peak, falls below zero into a broad shallow minimum, then creeps back up toward zero at large r. A dot sits at the minimum. Right: a circle centred on a dot representing the star.
figures.what_it_teaches: Effective energy equal to the potential minimum means no radial motion, hence a circular orbit; the inner peak and plunge are new compared with Newton.

redesign.idea: Effective-potential orbit explorer: left panel V_eff(r) for adjustable M and L-tilde with a draggable energy line; right panel integrates the Schwarzschild geodesic in real time and draws the orbit. Newtonian V_eff can be overlaid as a dashed curve.
redesign.interaction: Drag the energy line and the starting radius; slider for L-tilde (watch the peak and well appear, merge at the ISCO, and vanish); toggle GR term on/off; buttons 'snap to minimum' and 'snap to peak' for circular orbits.

figures.label: Fig. 14.2(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: An unbound particle with energy just below the potential peak comes in, swings around the star and escapes.
figures.visual_description: Same potential curve. A horizontal energy line at positive height just below the top of the peak starts at a dot on the outer flank of the peak and runs to the right. Right: a trajectory arrives from the upper left, wraps once around the central dot in a teardrop-shaped loop, and heads off toward the upper right. (The inventory labels this image Fig. 14.3; it is panel (b) of Fig. 14.2.)
figures.what_it_teaches: The outer flank of the peak acts as a turning point for incoming particles; energies near the peak produce whirls around the star before scattering.

redesign.idea: In the orbit explorer, a 'zoom-whirl' preset: fire particles from infinity with fixed L-tilde and energies approaching the peak, showing the number of loops growing without bound as E approaches the peak value.
redesign.interaction: Fine slider for E just below the peak with a logarithmic readout of (E_peak - E); counter of revolutions before escape; compare with Newtonian hyperbola.

figures.label: Fig. 14.2(c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: With energy above the peak, nothing stops the particle and it spirals into the star.
figures.visual_description: Same potential curve. A horizontal energy line well above the peak begins at a dot on the vertical axis and extends right, clearing the barrier entirely. Right: a curve comes down from the top and curls inward into a tightening spiral at the centre; unlike panels (a) and (b), no separate star dot is drawn.
figures.what_it_teaches: The relativistic 1/r^3 term removes the Newtonian guarantee of a centrifugal wall: sufficiently energetic or low angular momentum particles are captured.

redesign.idea: Capture-versus-escape map: a 2D parameter plane of (L-tilde, E) coloured by outcome (bound, scattered, captured) computed from V_eff, with a cursor linked to the orbit explorer.
redesign.interaction: Click anywhere on the (L-tilde, E) plane to launch the corresponding orbit; hover to see the potential with that energy line.

figures.label: Fig. 14.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: A bound orbit oscillates between two turning radii, and because the ellipse rotates it traces a rosette confined between two circles.
figures.visual_description: Left: the effective potential with a horizontal energy line below zero inside the well; dots mark where it meets the inner and outer walls. Right: three or four large, overlapping, offset near-circular loops around a central dot, enclosed by an outer dotted circle, with a small circle around the centre marking the inner turning radius; the two radii correspond to the turning points on the left.
figures.what_it_teaches: Perihelion precession: radial oscillation between fixed turning points combined with an angular period that does not match, so the orbit does not close. The drawing hugely exaggerates the effect compared with Mercury.

redesign.idea: Precession dial: a bound orbit drawn with fading trail, with the GR term's strength (or M/r_peri) adjustable from Mercury-like to near the innermost stable orbit; a counter shows precession angle per orbit and extrapolates to arcseconds per century for Mercury parameters.
redesign.interaction: Slider for compactness from 1e-8 to 0.15; toggle 'exaggerate' so learners see real Mercury precession is invisible per orbit; mark successive perihelia with dots; compare to the formula 6 pi GM/(c^2 a(1-e^2)).

worked_examples.label: Example 14.1
worked_examples.problem: Show how the perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor simplifies, with factors of c restored, for matter in the weak-field regime.
worked_examples.method: Estimate pressure as rho v^2 (kinetic energy density of particles), compare p/c^2 with rho, drop it, then use u^0 >> u^i to rank components.
worked_examples.key_insight: Ordinary matter in weak gravity is effectively pressureless dust; its gravitating content is dominated by rest-mass energy density.
worked_examples.result: T^{mu nu} ~ rho u^mu u^nu with T^{00} = rho c^2 >> T^{ii}.

worked_examples.label: Example 14.2
worked_examples.problem: Solve the linearized field equation for a slowly moving Newtonian source and find the resulting metric.
worked_examples.method: Keep only T_00 = rho (c = 1); discard time derivatives in the d'Alembertian; note the other h-bar components are sourceless and vanish at infinity; match del^2 h-bar_00 = -16 pi G rho to del^2 Phi = 4 pi G rho; compute the trace h-bar = 4 Phi; invert the trace reversal with explicit diagonal matrices; add to eta.
worked_examples.key_insight: Although only one component of h-bar is non-zero, undoing the trace reversal spreads -2 Phi into every diagonal slot, so space is perturbed as much as time.
worked_examples.result: h-bar_00 = -4 Phi; h_{mu nu} = diag(-2Phi,-2Phi,-2Phi,-2Phi); ds^2 = -(1+2Phi)dt^2 + (1-2Phi)(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2), eqns 14.8-14.10, proving eqn 5.22.

worked_examples.label: Example 14.3
worked_examples.problem: Explain why tidal distortion of a free-falling sphere near a planet preserves volume, and what the same reasoning implies for gravitational waves.
worked_examples.method: Use the component field equation's locality: T = 0 at a point makes R_{mu nu} vanish there. Interpret Ricci as the volume-changing part of curvature, so contraction and stretching must balance. For a planet one stretch balances two half-size squeezes; for a wave one stretch balances one equal squeeze.
worked_examples.key_insight: Volume conservation of vacuum tides is not a coincidence of Newtonian gravity but a direct statement of the vacuum Einstein equation; gravitational waves inherit the same budget.
worked_examples.result: Vacuum implies R_{mu nu} = 0; tidal ellipsoid has equal volume; a gravitational wave stretches one transverse direction and squeezes the perpendicular one by the same amount.
concepts: Ricci tensor as the volume-changing part of curvature

worked_examples.label: Example 14.4
worked_examples.problem: Build intuition for solutions of wave equations for fields with increasing numbers of indices, as a lead-in to gravitational waves.
worked_examples.method: Write the scalar wave equation in components and its plane-wave solution with omega = c|k|; repeat for a 1-form A_mu with a polarization amplitude C_mu; recall how E and B follow from the potentials.
worked_examples.key_insight: Polarization is the pattern of relative component amplitudes; more indices allow richer polarization structure, which for the two-index h-bar gives the stretch-squeeze patterns.
worked_examples.result: phi = C e^{-i(omega t - k.x)}; A_mu = Re[C_mu e^{-i(omega t - k.x)}]; E = -grad A^0 - dA/dt, B = curl A; leading to h-bar_{mu nu} = Re[A_{mu nu} e^{ik.x}].

worked_examples.problem: Embedded in margin note 5: restore factors of c in the Newtonian-limit results.
worked_examples.method: Dimensional analysis: T^{00} must be an energy density (rho c^2), Phi must appear as the dimensionless Phi/c^2, and the coupling 16 pi G/c^4 times rho c^2 gives 16 pi G rho/c^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Setting c = 1 hides that every metric correction is Phi/c^2, which is exactly the weak-field parameter GM/(r c^2).

worked_examples.problem: Embedded in the §14.1 prose: turn 'slow motion' into a condition on the gravitational field.
worked_examples.method: Require |u|^2/c^2 << 1; note speeds acquired by falling in a potential satisfy v^2 of order GM/r; combine to a dimensionless field strength.
worked_examples.key_insight: Weak gravity and slow motion are one approximation, not two, for bodies moving under gravity alone.
worked_examples.result: Weak-field condition GM/(r c^2) << 1 (printed with a dimensional slip as (GM/rc)^2 << 1).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Learning GR as climbing a mountain, with the field equation engraved at the summit and this chapter as the rest stop to admire the view.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Signals that the heavy construction is over and that what follows are payoffs, re-energizing the reader.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Purely motivational; it can suggest the field equation is the end point when much of GR's difficulty lies in solving and interpreting it.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: A course map rendered as a mountain with chapters as trail markers; the summit opens a panoramic 'triumphs' screen linking to demos for waves, orbits and cosmology.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravitational waves are like electromagnetic waves: both fields obey wave equations, have plane-wave solutions and polarization.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Used to make the existence of metric waves plausible and to organize Example 14.4 as a ladder from scalar to vector to tensor waves.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: GWs are spin-2 and quadrupolar (no dipole radiation), polarizations differ by 45 rather than 90 degrees, the coupling is vastly weaker, and the full theory is non-linear; gauge freedom is far richer.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side animation: EM wave moving a ring of charges versus GW moving a ring of masses, with sliders for polarization angle showing the 90 versus 45 degree difference.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A passing gravitational wave acts like a travelling tide, stretching and squeezing a ring of masses much as a planet's tidal field deforms a falling sphere.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Example 14.3 reuses the Chapter 11 tidal ellipsoid to explain the wave's stretch-squeeze pattern and its area balance.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The planet's tidal field is static and three-dimensional (one stretch, two squeezes); a wave's is oscillating, transverse and two-dimensional; neither is a force in GR, only geodesic deviation.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Toggle between 'planet tide' (3D ellipsoid, static) and 'gravitational wave' (2D ring, oscillating) with a shared stretch/squeeze budget bar that always sums to zero.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Ricci tensor as a kind of average of Riemann curvature that keeps only the volume-shrinking part.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: Ricci tensor as the volume-changing part of curvature
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note 7 uses it to connect vacuum R_{mu nu} = 0 to volume-preserving tides.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Contraction is a trace, not an average in the statistical sense; the statement holds for the second time derivative of volume of an initially comoving ball, and the leftover shape-changing part (Weyl) is not named.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ball of dust in free fall with a split readout: volume acceleration (Ricci part) and shear (Weyl part) as the learner moves the ball from inside a star to vacuum.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Orbital radial motion treated as a bead rolling in a one-dimensional effective potential valley.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Lets the reader classify orbits (circular, bound, scatter, capture) by drawing a horizontal energy line on V_eff, as in Figs 14.2-14.3.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'energy' is an effective constant per unit mass, the time variable is proper time, the potential itself depends on angular momentum, and the angular motion is hidden.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Marble-in-a-valley animation synchronized with the actual 2D orbit; changing L-tilde reshapes the valley in real time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Pressure pictured as particles with kinetic energy bouncing off container walls, so its size is roughly density times speed squared.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note 3 justifies p ~ rho v^2, hence p/c^2 << rho for slow matter.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Order-of-magnitude only; ignores numerical factors and fails for radiation or degenerate matter where internal speeds approach c.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Gas-in-a-box simulation with a speed slider showing p/(rho c^2) as a live bar that stays tiny until speeds approach c.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The scale factor a(t) as an effective radius of the Universe.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a concrete handle on what the Robertson-Walker dynamics describe.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a literal radius for a closed (k = +1) universe; for flat or open models the space may be infinite and a(t) is a relative stretching factor between comoving points.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Comoving grid of galaxies whose spacing scales with a(t), rendered on a sphere, plane, or saddle depending on k, to show a is a stretch factor, not an edge.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The perturbation h_{mu nu} is a genuine tensor field on spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It transforms as a tensor under Lorentz transformations of the flat background, but under small coordinate changes it shifts by gauge terms (partial_mu xi_nu + partial_nu xi_mu), and its indices are moved with eta rather than g.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It has two indices, is written like every other tensor, and is part of g which is a tensor.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In vacuum spacetime is flat, since the field equation sets curvature to zero where there is no matter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the Ricci part vanishes in vacuum; the Riemann tensor can be non-zero, producing tides near planets and gravitational waves far from sources.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The informal slogan 'matter tells spacetime how to curve' suggests no matter means no curvature.
concepts: Ricci tensor as the volume-changing part of curvature

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Newtonian limit only modifies g_00; the spatial metric stays flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Solving the linearized equations gives the same -2 Phi perturbation in every diagonal component, so g_ij = (1 - 2Phi) delta_ij. Slow particles are insensitive to it, but light is not: it supplies half of the solar deflection.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian dynamics of slow bodies can be derived from g_00 alone, as in earlier chapters.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Slow motion alone guarantees the Newtonian limit.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: One also needs weak potentials, slowly varying sources, and negligible pressure and stresses (p << rho c^2); for neutron stars or radiation-dominated matter pressure itself gravitates.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The section starts from velocity conditions and then equates them to weak fields.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A gravitational wave squeezes or stretches everything uniformly, or acts along its direction of travel.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The effect is transverse and traceless: in the plane perpendicular to propagation one direction stretches while the perpendicular one squeezes equally, and the pattern reverses each half period; nothing happens along the propagation direction at linear order.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Sound waves are longitudinal and 'ripples in spacetime' sounds like uniform expansion and contraction.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: All sixteen (or ten) components of the gravitational wave amplitude are physical degrees of freedom.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Symmetry leaves 10, coordinate (gauge) freedom removes 8 more, leaving 2 physical polarizations, the two shown in Fig. 14.1.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text emphasizes the count of 16 and only reduces it to 10.
concepts: independent components of a symmetric tensor

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Mercury's whole perihelion precession is a relativistic effect.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Observed precession is about 575 arcsec per century, most of it from other planets' pulls; GR accounts for the residual 43 arcsec that Newtonian models could not explain.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter quotes only the 43 arcsec figure as the precession.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian gravity predicts no bending of light at all.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Treating light as fast particles in Newtonian gravity gives a deflection half the GR value; GR's doubling comes from the spatial part of the metric.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text says light bending is a contrast with Newtonian theory.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The drawn precessing rosette shows how Mercury's orbit looks.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The figure is exaggerated by many orders of magnitude; Mercury's perihelion advances by roughly 0.1 arcsec per orbit.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Textbook orbit sketches rarely state their scale.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big Bang was an explosion from a point located somewhere in pre-existing space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a singular limit of the whole spacetime geometry where a(t) -> 0 everywhere; in flat or open models space may be infinite even arbitrarily close to it, and there is no centre.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Phrases like 'the whole universe shrunk to a point' and 'effective radius' invite a picture of a small ball in space.

thought_experiments.name: Ring of free test masses in a passing gravitational wave
thought_experiments.setup: Place free masses on a circle in empty space, perpendicular to the direction a gravitational wave travels, and watch their separations as the wave passes.
thought_experiments.lesson: The ring deforms into an ellipse that alternates orientation each half period, with two independent polarization patterns; distances are what change, which is how interferometers detect waves.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Ring lab with adjustable plus/cross amplitudes, exaggeration factor and an overlaid L-shaped interferometer reporting arm-length difference.

thought_experiments.name: Falling ball of dust above a planet
thought_experiments.setup: Release a small spherical cloud of free particles above a planet and follow its shape as it falls, comparing with a cloud in a gravitational wave.
thought_experiments.lesson: The cloud becomes an ellipsoid of the same volume because vacuum is Ricci-flat; a wave does the same bookkeeping in two dimensions.
thought_experiments.app_idea: 3D dust ball with volume readout; move it inside a uniform-density planet to watch volume start to shrink when matter is present.

thought_experiments.name: Marble in the relativistic effective potential
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine a particle with fixed angular momentum and some effective energy moving in V_eff(r); vary the energy relative to the well and the inner peak.
thought_experiments.lesson: Energy placement relative to the well minimum and inner peak decides circular, precessing bound, scattering or capture motion, unlike the Newtonian potential which always has a centrifugal wall.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Linked V_eff plot and orbit integrator with draggable energy line and Newtonian/GR toggle.

historical_notes.event: First direct detection of gravitational waves: a burst lasting about 150 ms attributed to two merging black holes.
historical_notes.significance: Confirmed a century-old prediction and showed only enormously powerful events produce detectable strain.

historical_notes.event: Relativistic prediction of the anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury (about 43 arcsec per century), cited as one of the earliest triumphs of the theory. Year added by us.
historical_notes.significance: Explained a long-standing residual in Newtonian celestial mechanics without adjustable parameters.

historical_notes.event: Prediction of elliptical planetary orbits in an inverse-square central potential, set as the baseline GR enriches.
historical_notes.significance: Frames GR's orbital predictions as corrections to a celebrated success.

historical_notes.event: Exact spherically symmetric vacuum solution, quoted here as eqn 14.17. Year added by us.
historical_notes.significance: Basis of all classical Solar System tests and of black-hole physics.

historical_notes.event: The homogeneous isotropic cosmological metric quoted as eqn 14.20. Years added by us.
historical_notes.significance: Standard geometric framework for modern cosmology developed in Part III.

applications_and_observations.details: Precession of Mercury's near-elliptical orbit predicted by the relativistic effective potential agrees with observation; historically decisive. Context from GA ch23 and standard data (not stated in this chapter): total observed advance about 575 arcsec/century, of which about 532 comes from planetary perturbations.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: GR prediction ~43.0 arcsec per century (book); observed residual 43.1 +/- 0.5 arcsec per century (GA ch23)

applications_and_observations.topic: LIGO detection of a binary black hole merger
applications_and_observations.details: Gravitational waves escaped detection until 2015 when the two LIGO interferometers recorded a short burst from colliding black holes. Our additions: event GW150914 (14 Sept 2015, announced Feb 2016), component masses about 36 and 29 solar masses, peak strain about 1e-21, roughly 3 solar masses of energy radiated.

Perihelion precession, deflection of starlight by the Sun, and gravitational redshift are listed as the three classical tests. Our additions: solar-limb deflection 1.75 arcsec (Eddington 1919 expeditions); Pound-Rebka tower redshift experiment 1959-1960 with fractional shift ~2.5e-15.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Light deflection at solar limb 1.75 arcsec (our addition)

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the weak-field parameter GM/(r c^2)
applications_and_observations.details: Our own estimates to show when the Newtonian limit applies: Earth's surface ~7e-10, Sun's surface ~2e-6, white dwarf ~1e-4, neutron star surface ~0.2, black-hole horizon 0.5.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Sun: GM/(R c^2) ~ 2.1e-6; neutron star ~0.2 (our estimates)

applications_and_observations.details: An effective potential for light rays in Schwarzschild geometry predicts bending and hence lensing of background sources by foreground masses.
Very dense mass distributions in the Schwarzschild geometry lead to regions from which light cannot escape; developed in Part IV.
Robertson-Walker models filled with different matter have different histories, many starting from a singular Big Bang followed by expansion; developed in Part III.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (-,+,+,+): eta_{mu nu} = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1), visible in the matrices of eqns 14.8-14.9.
SI with factors of c and G shown in eqns 14.1, 14.4, 14.17, 14.19, 14.20; c = 1 inside Example 14.2 and eqns 14.6-14.10, with SI versions collected in margin note 5 as eqn (14.5).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Eqn (14.5) is tagged in the margin and so appears out of numerical order.

notation_and_conventions.convention: partial^2 = eta^{mu nu} partial_mu partial_nu = -(1/c^2) partial_t^2 + del^2.
h_{mu nu} indices raised/lowered with eta; h without indices is the trace eta^{mu nu} h_{mu nu}; overbar denotes trace reversal.
Bold G and T denote the Einstein and energy-momentum tensors as geometric objects; components written with indices.
R_{mu nu} = R^alpha_{mu alpha nu} (contraction on first and third slots).
In Example 14.3 'positive curvature' refers to tidal contraction and 'negative curvature' to stretching.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Heuristic usage; not a formal sign convention for Riemann components.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Physical waves are real parts of complex exponentials; k.x in e^{ik.x} is the four-vector product -omega t + k.x.
Script E is the conserved effective energy per unit mass; L-tilde the angular momentum per unit mass; figures label axes V_eff(r-vector) against |r-vector|.

difficulty.notes: Deliberately light: the only real derivation (Example 14.2) is short matrix algebra once eqn 14.4 is granted, and the rest is quoted results with pictures. Conceptual load comes from breadth (waves, Ricci-flatness, orbits, cosmology in six pages) and from key steps asserted without justification: the linearized equation itself, the gauge condition it needs, why h is not a tensor, and why only two polarizations exist. There are no exercises. Printed slips (the dimensionally inconsistent weak-field criterion and c factors in eqns 14.18-14.19) could confuse a careful reader.
