teaching_gems.gem: Undo the trace reversal with explicit matrices: diag(-4Phi,0,0,0) minus (1/2)(4Phi) eta equals -2Phi times the identity, so a perturbation that lived only in the time slot spreads equally into space.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The surprise that space is perturbed as much as time is visible arithmetic rather than an assertion; a tutor can extend it (the book does not) to explain why GR light bending is twice the Newtonian corpuscle estimate.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Animated matrix subtraction: the h-bar matrix, the scaled eta matrix, and their difference fill in cell by cell; a toggle then shows the effect of the spatial -2Phi on a light ray's deflection (with versus without).

teaching_gems.gem: Get the coupling constant by matching: the static 00 component of the linearized equation is Poisson's equation in disguise, so Newton fixes h-bar_00 = -4Phi.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows concretely how Newtonian gravity sits inside GR as one component of one equation in one limit.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two stacked equations with matched terms highlighted; learner drags the unknown factor until both equations agree for a sample density profile, with a plot of Phi and h-bar_00 overlaid.

teaching_gems.gem: Slow motion equals weak field: speeds acquired by falling satisfy v^2 ~ GM/r, so both conditions are the single parameter GM/(r c^2).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Reduces two approximations to one number learners can estimate for Earth, Sun and neutron stars.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Compactness ladder: slider through objects (Earth, Sun, white dwarf, neutron star, black hole) displaying GM/(r c^2) on a log scale with a shaded 'Newton works' region.

teaching_gems.gem: Ricci-flat budget: planet tides stretch one axis and squeeze two by half as much; a gravitational wave stretches one and squeezes one equally; in both cases vacuum Einstein forces the total to zero.
teaching_gems.why_effective: One principle explains both a familiar Newtonian fact and the unfamiliar wave pattern, and it previews what the Ricci tensor physically measures.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Stretch-squeeze budget bars beside a 3D dust ball (planet) and a 2D ring (wave); the bars always sum to zero in vacuum, and entering matter makes the sum negative.

teaching_gems.gem: Ring of test masses with displacement arrows from the undisturbed circle, shown at two instants half a period apart and for two polarizations.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Arrows make the displacement field explicit (radial on some axes, tangential on others), which carries the shear nature of the wave better than ellipses alone.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive ring lab with plus/cross sliders, phase scrubber, arrow toggle, and an interferometer overlay reading arm-length difference.

teaching_gems.gem: Climb a ladder of wave equations: scalar, then 1-form with a polarization vector, then symmetric two-index field, so polarization structure grows with the number of indices.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Leverages electromagnetism learners already know and prepares the idea that gravitational polarization is a tensor pattern.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Three synchronized panels (scalar height field, EM field arrows, GW ring) driven by one wavevector control; learner rotates the polarization and compares symmetry angles.

teaching_gems.gem: Pair every effective-potential sketch with its orbit and mark the turning points: the single relativistic 1/r^3 term creates an inner peak that allows capture and makes bound orbits precess.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Lets learners reason about orbits qualitatively from one graph and isolates exactly what GR adds to Newton.
teaching_gems.app_idea: V_eff explorer with Newton/GR toggle, draggable energy line and live geodesic integration showing circular, precessing, scattering, zoom-whirl and plunging orbits.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The weak-field condition is printed as (GM/rc)^2 << 1, which has dimensions of speed squared; the dimensionless parameter is GM/(r c^2).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A reader checking units finds a contradiction right where the text urges restoring c.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the criterion as GM/(r c^2) << 1, equivalently v^2/c^2 << 1 with v^2 ~ GM/r.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqns 14.18-14.19 mix unit conventions: V_eff as printed is dimensionless while (1/2)(dr/dtau)^2 has units of speed squared.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who plug in SI numbers get nonsense or lose trust in the formula.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Work in G = c = 1 (GA eqns 22.22-22.23), or keep V_eff as printed (it equals GA eqn 22.24) and write the kinetic term as (1/(2c^2))(dr/dtau)^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The linearized equation 14.4 is quoted without derivation and silently assumes the Lorenz (harmonic) gauge; the non-tensor nature of h is asserted but unexplained.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may believe any small perturbation obeys the simple wave equation and be confused later by gauge terms.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a sentence that coordinate freedom lets one impose partial^mu h-bar_{mu nu} = 0, and show a two-line example of h shifting under x -> x + xi; point to GA ch45 §45.3.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Newtonian-limit derivation keeps only T_00 and drops time derivatives without spelling out the conditions (p << rho c^2, slowly varying sources, small stresses) or noting that the -2Phi spatial part is physically meaningful.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may apply the weak-field metric to relativistic stars or think the spatial part is a bookkeeping artefact.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: List the three approximations explicitly and connect the spatial -2Phi to the factor 2 in light deflection.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Only the reduction 16 -> 10 components is mentioned; the transverse-traceless structure and the fact that exactly two physical polarizations remain are not explained, yet Fig. 14.1 shows two.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot see why there are two patterns or why they differ by 45 degrees.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Briefly count: 10 minus 4 gauge conditions minus 4 residual freedoms leaves 2; show the plus and cross matrices in transverse-traceless gauge.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 14.3's physical argument uses informal sign language ('positive curvature' for contraction) and glosses that Ricci-flatness constrains the second time derivative of volume for an initially comoving ball.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may conflate this heuristic with the sign conventions of Riemann components or with spatial curvature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Phrase it as the Raychaudhuri-type statement that the volume acceleration of a small dust ball is proportional to R_{mu nu} u^mu u^nu, zero in vacuum.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 14.1 and Fig. 14.3 exaggerate amplitudes enormously (ring distortion tens of percent versus strain ~1e-21; precession ~90 degrees per orbit versus ~0.1 arcsec for Mercury) without saying so.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Novices form wrong intuitions about how detectable these effects are.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add scale notes or, in the app, an 'exaggeration factor' slider that can be set to realistic values.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The LIGO paragraph is minimal (no strain, distance, masses, or later events such as the 2017 neutron-star merger with electromagnetic counterpart).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Loses a strong motivational hook and quantitative sense of the achievement.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Supplement with GW150914 key numbers and a timeline of detections; defer interferometer physics to GA ch46 §46.6.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text contrasts light bending with Newtonian theory and describes the Big Bang as the Universe shrunk to a point and a(t) as a radius.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Seeds the misconceptions that Newton predicts no deflection and that the Big Bang was an explosion at a place in space.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mention the half-size Newtonian deflection and describe the Big Bang as a(t) -> 0 everywhere, with a as a stretch factor between comoving points.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Minor typos in §14.3: 'The line element of his metric' (Schwarzschild's name dropped), 'affects' for effects, 'Here's we'll', lowercase 'mercury'.

gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners get no practice deriving the weak-field metric or reading effective-potential plots.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide short practice items: redo Example 14.2 in SI, compute GM/(r c^2) for several bodies, sketch V_eff for several L-tilde values and classify orbits.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'We finally have the field equation. What would convince you it is right?' Steer toward three answers: it must reduce to Newton, it must predict something new that is observed, and it must describe the Universe as a whole. That is exactly the chapter's structure.
Before Example 14.2, check that the learner can do a trace reversal on a diagonal 4x4 matrix with signature (-,+,+,+); many errors come from forgetting eta_00 = -1 when computing the trace.

Teach the Newtonian limit in this order: (1) one small parameter GM/(r c^2); (2) dust source; (3) g = eta + h and h-bar; (4) static 00 component equals Poisson; (5) undo trace reversal; (6) read off the metric and ask what the spatial part is for.
Correct the printed weak-field criterion on the fly: say GM/(r c^2), and ask the learner to check units themselves as a quick understanding check.
Check for understanding: 'If h-bar has only a 00 component, why does h have four non-zero components?' and 'Which part of the weak-field metric does a slow planet feel, and which does light feel?'

For gravitational waves, first recall the Chapter 11 tidal ellipsoid, then ask the learner to predict what a transverse, volume-preserving distortion in a plane must look like before showing the ring figure.

Common learner question: 'If the wave stretches space, why doesn't the laser light stretch too so LIGO sees nothing?' Answer briefly that the light's travel time between free mirrors changes during the passage because the wave period is long compared with that time; defer details to GA ch46.
Common learner question: 'Why only two polarizations?' Acknowledge the chapter stops at 10 components, then give the gauge-counting sketch (10 - 4 - 4 = 2) at a level matching the learner.

For orbits, have the learner draw an energy line on V_eff for each of: circular, precessing bound, scattering, capture, and describe the orbit before revealing Figs 14.2-14.3; then toggle off the 1/r^3 term and ask what disappears.
Quote realistic magnitudes whenever figures are exaggerated: Mercury ~43 arcsec/century (~0.1 arcsec per orbit), LIGO strain ~1e-21.
Keep cosmology short here: interpret a(t) as a stretch factor and k as spatial curvature, warn against the 'explosion at a point' picture, and point forward to Part III.
Use units carefully in §14.3: work with G = c = 1 for V_eff, or divide eqn 14.18 by c^2 if SI is needed.
